chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Wasir, from Ismail ibn Sahl, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) left Medina in the remaining days of Sha'ban, and he would fast. Then the month of Ramadan entered upon him while he was traveling, so he broke his fast. He was asked: 'You fast in Sha'ban but break your fast in the month of Ramadan?' He said: 'Yes, Sha'ban is up to me; if I wish I fast, and if I wish I do not. And the month of Ramadan is a divine obligation upon me to break the fast [i.e., to perform the obligatory fast].'

key_terms.رَمَضَان: Ramadan, the ninth month of fasting
key_terms.شَعْبَان: Sha'ban, the eighth month of the Islamic lunar calendar

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fasting in Sha'ban versus Ramadan while traveling according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies the distinction between voluntary (nafl) and obligatory (fard) fasting for travelers, with Imam al-Sadiq (AS) demonstrating that while Sha'ban fasting is discretionary, Ramadan fasting is a divine command (azm) that travelers must observe before breaking it. It highlights the scholarly principle that the obligation of Ramadan fasting remains in effect during travel, with breaking the fast being the concession rather than the default state, contrasting with the flexibility of voluntary acts. This ruling is foundational in Shia fiqh for understanding the hierarchy of obligations versus supererogatory acts in the context of travel.
